name: man
summary: Read the manual page for a command, system call, C library function or config file.

install.note: Minimal container images often strip man pages. Section 2/3 pages for C come from the manpages-dev (Debian/Ubuntu) or man-pages (Fedora, Arch, Alpine) package.

compat: Manual sections: 1 user commands, 2 system calls, 3 C library functions, 4 devices, 5 file formats, 7 overviews, 8 administration commands. Embedded/BusyBox systems usually ship no man pages at all, so read them on your development machine.

examples.title: Open the manual for a command
examples.explain: Opens the page in a pager (usually less). Use arrow keys or Space to scroll, / to search, q to quit.
options: Name of the command, e.g. ls or tar

examples.title: Read a C library function, not the shell command of the same name
examples.explain: Without a section number you get printf(1), the shell command. Section 3 is the C library function you call from C code, including its #include line and return value.
options: Manual section 3: C library functions (2 = system calls such as open, read, ioctl)

examples.title: Read the documentation for a system call
examples.explain: Section 2 describes kernel system calls: arguments, flags such as O_RDONLY, and every errno value the call can return. Very useful when a C program fails with an error code.

examples.title: Search manual page descriptions by keyword
examples.explain: Lists pages whose short description mentions the keyword. Same as the apropos command. Prints 'nothing appropriate' if the index is missing or empty.

name: type
summary: Show whether a name is a shell builtin, alias, function or a program on disk (and which one runs).

install.note: Built into the shell; there is nothing to install.

compat: type -a is a Bash feature. In plain POSIX sh (dash, BusyBox ash) use command -v, which is portable.

examples.title: Find out what a name refers to
examples.explain: Prints for example 'cd is a shell builtin'. Builtins have no separate man page; read them with help cd in Bash.

examples.title: List every match, in the order the shell tries them
examples.explain: Shows aliases first (e.g. 'ls is aliased to ls --color=auto') and then each matching file in PATH. The first line is what actually runs.
options: Show all aliases, functions, builtins and files with this name

examples.title: Portable check whether a program exists
examples.explain: Prints the path (or the name, for builtins) and exits with status 0 if found; prints nothing and exits non-zero if not. Works in sh scripts: command -v gcc >/dev/null || echo 'gcc missing'.
options: Print how the name would be resolved instead of running it

name: echo
summary: Print text and variable values; with redirection, write text into files.

install.note: Every shell has an echo builtin; /bin/echo also exists from coreutils or BusyBox.

compat: Options such as -e and -n behave differently between bash, dash and BusyBox. For anything beyond plain text, printf is more predictable.

examples.title: Print a variable inside double quotes
examples.explain: Double quotes let the shell expand $USER but keep the text as one argument. Without quotes, extra spaces collapse and wildcard characters may expand.

examples.title: Print text literally with single quotes
examples.explain: Inside single quotes nothing is expanded: no variables, no wildcards. Use single quotes when you mean the exact characters.

examples.title: Overwrite vs append to a file
examples.cmd: echo 'first line' > notes-out.txt && echo 'second line' >> notes-out.txt
examples.explain: > creates the file or silently REPLACES all of its contents. >> creates it or adds to the end. && runs the second command only if the first succeeded.
examples.warning: A single > on an existing file erases what was there. Double-check the file name; in Bash, set -o noclobber makes > refuse to overwrite.
options: Redirect output, truncating (emptying) the file first
Redirect output, appending to the end
Run the next command only if the previous one exited with status 0

name: printf
summary: Print formatted text using C-style format strings; more portable than echo.

install.note: Builtin in bash, dash and BusyBox ash; /usr/bin/printf comes from coreutils.

compat: Format specifiers work like C printf(3) but there is no automatic newline: add \n yourself.

examples.title: Print a value followed by a newline
examples.explain: %s is replaced by the next argument; \n adds the newline. If you give more arguments than placeholders, the format is reused for each one.
options: Insert the next argument as a string

examples.title: Convert decimal to hexadecimal
examples.explain: Prints ff. Handy when reading register values or addresses. Use %X for upper case or %#x to get the 0x prefix.

examples.title: Align columns
examples.explain: %-10s pads the text to 10 characters, left-aligned; %5d right-aligns a number in 5 characters. The format is repeated for each pair of arguments.

name: export
summary: Set environment variables that are passed to programs you start (PATH, CC, ARCH, CROSS_COMPILE...).

install.note: export is a shell builtin; env and printenv come from coreutils or BusyBox.

compat: Variables set with export last only for the current shell session and programs started from it. To make them permanent add the line to ~/.bashrc (Bash) or ~/.profile.

examples.title: Add a directory to the front of PATH
examples.explain: Programs in the new directory are found before system ones. Keep :$PATH at the end, otherwise you lose access to every other command in this shell.
examples.warning: Writing PATH="something" without :$PATH replaces the whole search path for this shell. Open a new terminal to recover.
options: Colon-separated list of directories searched for commands

examples.title: Set a variable for one command only
examples.explain: VAR=value before a command sets the variable just for that command. Here it makes sort use plain byte order regardless of your language settings.

examples.title: Print one environment variable
examples.explain: Prints the value, or nothing (exit status 1) if the variable is not set or not exported.

examples.title: List all environment variables, sorted
examples.explain: env with no arguments prints NAME=value for every exported variable. Be careful when sharing this output: it can contain tokens or passwords.

name: alias
summary: Create short names for longer commands in your interactive shell.
compat: Aliases only apply to interactive shells by default, not to scripts. Put permanent aliases in ~/.bashrc.

examples.title: Show all current aliases
examples.explain: Many distributions predefine aliases such as ll or ls --color=auto. This is why a command may behave differently on another machine.

examples.title: Define an alias for this session
examples.explain: Typing ll now runs ls -alF. Use single quotes so nothing inside is expanded when the alias is defined.

examples.title: Remove an alias
examples.explain: Deletes the alias from the current shell only. It comes back in new shells if it is defined in ~/.bashrc.

name: history
summary: List and search commands you ran earlier in the shell.

install.note: Bash builtin. BusyBox ash has a simpler history if built with that feature.

compat: Press Ctrl+R in Bash and type part of an old command to search history interactively; press Ctrl+R again for older matches.

examples.title: Show the last 20 commands
examples.explain: Each line starts with a number. !<number> re-runs that entry, so check what it is first.

examples.title: Find an old command by keyword
examples.explain: Pipes the whole history into grep. Useful for recovering a long gcc or make command you typed earlier.
